How to make your own South Park character.

A few thoughtful choices are enough to create a recognizable avatar. Start simple, then adjust the details that make it yours.

01
Choose your starting point

Open the free studio and select a preset that is close to your idea. Look at the overall silhouette rather than searching for a perfect match. A hairstyle or an outfit color can be changed later. If you would rather explore an imagined scene, switch to the AI generator and describe the character you have in mind.

02
Give the details a purpose

Try hair, hats, clothing, and facial expressions one group at a time. Use the live preview to see how each change affects the character. Round glasses can suggest a book lover; a cap and a relaxed expression can suggest a weekend skater. Undo a change whenever an earlier version felt closer to your idea.

03
Download a version you love

Choose a background that suits the destination, then export a 1024 × 1024 PNG or an SVG. Save a copy to your device before leaving the page. The optional browser save keeps an editable version on this device, but it does not replace a downloaded backup or synchronize your designs across different browsers.

A little more character in every detail.

A South Park character maker turns a familiar cartoon language into a personal creative exercise. Round heads, clear expressions, compact bodies, and flat shapes make small design decisions easy to notice. The goal is an original avatar with a recognizable personality, rather than a copy of an existing television character. You do not need to draw to get started.

A familiar style. An original you.
Start with a recognizable silhouette

Hair and headwear set the first impression. Try a short cut, curls, long hair, a bob, or a spiky shape before adding accessories. If you are making a cartoon version of yourself, choose the feature people notice first. If you are inventing someone new, let the silhouette suggest a hobby, mood, or small backstory. Keep the design readable at a glance.

Use color to connect the look

Give your character a small color palette instead of choosing every detail separately. A familiar hoodie can become the anchor, with hair and accessories kept quieter. Warm clothing against a snowy scene feels different from a soft-colored outfit in the park. The editor lets you compare these combinations immediately, so you can make a choice by looking rather than guessing.

Let the expression tell the story

A smile, a calm face, a surprised look, and a grumpy expression can turn the same outfit into four different personalities. Think about where the avatar will appear. A welcoming expression may suit a profile picture, while a dramatic reaction may work better for an inside joke. Glasses and freckles add another layer without making the small character harder to read.

Keep the scene in balance

The background should support the character rather than compete with it. Use snowy mountains for the familiar small-town atmosphere, a park for a softer everyday scene, or plain paper when you want attention on the outfit. Choose a transparent background when placing the avatar into another design. You can return to the scene controls before exporting a different version.

Your avatar, outside the studio.

The best character is one you want to use. Plan its destination while you make it, so the expression, colors, and background work together.

Profile pictures

Use a simple background and a clear face for chat apps, community profiles, or a personal account. Preview the image at a small size before settling on tiny details.

Friends and inside jokes

Make a character inspired by a shared hobby, a favorite jacket, or a familiar expression. Use photos or likenesses only with permission, and keep the result considerate of the people involved.

Original character ideas

Build a small visual reference for a fictional personality. Change one decision at a time and save variations when different outfits or moods suggest a more interesting direction.

Stickers and small projects

A transparent export makes it easier to place your character on a card, a personal sticker layout, or a presentation. Check the requirements of the app or printer you use.

PNG
SVG
The right file for the next idea.

Download a PNG for a ready-to-use square image, or keep an SVG when you need artwork that can scale. Both come from the same character you see in the builder.

PNG, ready to share

The builder exports a 1024 × 1024 PNG. Select Transparent in the scene controls for a file without a background. Some profile-picture apps crop images into a circle, so leave room around the character when checking the result.

SVG, room to grow

SVG keeps the artwork as vector shapes. It is useful when resizing a character for a layout, although some apps accept only raster formats. Keep the original download and choose a format supported by the place you plan to use it.
